text: But I must quickly add that I, too, am just as guilty in the question of the single story. <break time="0.8s" /> A few years ago, I visited Mexico from the U, S. <break time="0.8s" /> The political climate in the U, S, at the time was tense. <break time="0.8s" /> And there were debates going on about immigration. <break time="0.8s" /> And, as often happens in America, immigration became synonymous with Mexicans. <break time="0.8s" /> There were endless stories of Mexicans as people who were fleecing the healthcare system, sneaking across the border, being arrested at the border, that sort of thing. <break time="0.8s" /> I remember walking around on my first day in Guadalajara, watching the people going to work, rolling up tortillas in the marketplace, smoking, laughing. <break time="0.8s" /> I remember first feeling slight surprise. <break time="0.8s" /> And then I was overwhelmed with shame. <break time="0.8s" /> I realized that I had been so immersed in the media coverage of Mexicans that they had become one thing in my mind, the abject immigrant. <break time="0.8s" /> I had bought into the single story of Mexicans and I could not have been more ashamed of myself. <break time="0.8s" /> So, that is how to create a single story, show a people as one thing, as only one thing, over and over again, and that is what they become. <break time="0.8s" /> It is impossible to talk about the single story without talking about power. <break time="0.8s" /> There is a word, an Igbo word, that I think about whenever I think about the power structures of the world, and it is nkali. <break time="0.8s" /> It is a noun that loosely translates to to be greater than another. <break time="0.8s" /> Like our economic and political worlds, stories too are defined by the principle of nkali. <break time="0.8s" /> How they are told, who tells them, when they are told, how many stories are told, are really dependent on power. <break time="0.8s" /> Power is the ability not just to tell the story of another person, but to make it the definitive story of that person. <break time="0.8s" /> The Palestinian poet Mourid Barghouti writes that if you want to dispossess a people, the simplest way to do it is to tell their story, and to start with, secondly. <break time="0.8s" /> Start the story with the arrows of the Native Americans, and not with the arrival of the British, and you have and entirely different story. <break time="0.8s" /> Start the story with the failure of the African state, and not with the colonial creation of the African state, and you have an entirely different story. <break time="0.8s" /> I recently spoke at a university where a student told me that it was such a shame that Nigerian men were physical abusers like the father character in my novel.
